facts.title: Hidden Inside Cerium
facts.text: Lanthanum was discovered in 1839 by Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander, who detected it as an impurity lurking in cerium nitrate. He had to repeatedly dissolve and decompose cerium salts to coax out the new oxide, revealing that what chemists thought was one element was actually a mixture.

facts.title: A Name That Means 'Hidden'
facts.text: The element's name comes from the Greek word 'lanthanein', meaning 'to lie hidden' or 'to escape notice'. It was a fitting tribute, since lanthanum had concealed itself within cerium compounds and went unnoticed for decades after cerium itself was identified in 1803.

facts.title: Head of a Whole Family
facts.text: Lanthanum is the namesake of the entire lanthanide series, the 15 elements from atomic number 57 to 71. Although it sits at the front of the f-block, lanthanum's neutral atom actually has no electrons in its 4f orbital, placing its lone valence electron in a 5d orbital instead, which makes it a slightly unusual leader of the group it defines.

facts.title: Boosts the Brilliance of Glass
facts.text: Lanthanum oxide dramatically raises the refractive index of glass while keeping dispersion low, so it is added to high-quality optical glass for camera lenses, binoculars, and telescopes. This 'lanthanum crown' glass lets manufacturers build sharper, more compact lenses, and historically made up a large share of lanthanum's industrial demand.

facts.title: Powering Hybrid Cars
facts.text: Each nickel-metal-hydride battery, like those in many early hybrid vehicles such as the Toyota Prius, can contain several kilograms of a mischmetal alloy rich in lanthanum. The metal forms hydrogen-absorbing compounds (LaNi5-type alloys) that store and release hydrogen reversibly, acting as the battery's negative electrode.

facts.title: A Medicine for the Kidneys
facts.text: Lanthanum carbonate is sold as the prescription drug Fosrenol to treat high phosphate levels in people with chronic kidney disease. Taken with meals, it binds dietary phosphate in the gut so the body cannot absorb it, preventing dangerous mineral buildup in patients on dialysis.

facts.title: Soft Enough to Cut
facts.text: Pure lanthanum is a silvery-white metal so soft that it can be cut with a knife, and it is one of the most reactive of the rare-earth metals. Exposed to air it tarnishes rapidly, and it reacts with water to release hydrogen gas, which is why it is often stored under mineral oil or inert atmosphere.

facts.title: Not So Rare After All
facts.text: Despite being called a rare-earth element, lanthanum is fairly abundant, making up roughly 39 parts per million of Earth's crust, more common than lead. It is mainly extracted from the minerals monazite and bastnasite, where it occurs alongside cerium and other lanthanides.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Lanthanum, like most heavy elements, is created in the cosmos through neutron-capture processes inside aging stars and stellar explosions. Astronomers even use the strength of lanthanum spectral lines to classify rare 'barium stars' and to probe the chemical history of our galaxy.

facts.title: The Glow Behind Old Lamps
facts.text: Lanthanum compounds were once central to gas-mantle and carbon-arc lighting, and lanthanum-doped phosphors helped produce intense studio and projector light. The element also serves as a catalyst in petroleum refining, where lanthanum-exchanged zeolites improve the cracking of crude oil into gasoline.
